| Level | Example | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| L0 read-only | debug, read logs, write docs | do it directly |
| L1 dev/sandbox, can be undone | test a component on a dev cluster | short plan → do → verify → change record |

# Git Workflow

## Commit Message Format
```
<type>: <description>

<optional body>
```

Types: feat, fix, refactor, docs, test, chore, perf, ci

Note: ECC-managed installs set `"includeCoAuthoredBy": false` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, so commits carry no `Co-Authored-By` trailer by default. To keep Claude attribution, set `"includeCoAuthoredBy": true` or configure `attribution`; ECC never overwrites an explicit choice.

## Pull Request Workflow

When creating PRs:
1. Analyze full commit history (not just latest commit)
2. Use `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to see all changes
3. Draft comprehensive PR summary
4. Include test plan with TODOs
5. Push with `-u` flag if new branch

# CLAUDE.md — Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1

## Purpose of this repo

This repository is my submission for Papaya's **DevSecOps Challenge 1 — "DevSecOps with
Coding Agents at Papaya"** (full text: `work/00-challenge.md`). The task is to design the
framework and workflow for how Papaya uses coding agents (Claude Code) for DevSecOps,
reconciling two positions:

- Engineering: "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly."
- Compliance: "Nothing changes in production without a named human who reviewed and approved it."

Two things make this repo unusual and shape every rule below:

1. **The complete, raw Claude Code session transcripts are part of the submission** and are
   graded. Work transparently: state the reason behind each recommendation, show trade-offs,
   and say so when something is unverified.
2. **I have no access to Papaya's systems or code**, and the challenge does not expect it.
   Everything is a design on top of the stack described in the challenge's Appendix A.

## Hard constraints from the brief

- Design for Papaya's existing stack: AWS (Lambda via Serverless Framework, ECS, EC2, Aurora
  PostgreSQL, SNS/SQS, Step Functions, S3, CloudWatch), GCP (Vertex AI, Gemini), k0s
  Kubernetes, Firebase Hosting, a single GitHub monorepo, GitHub Actions, Pulumi, Claude Code
  (Team Premium) with an internal plugin marketplace, Linear, Slack.
- **Do not propose replacing IaC or CI tooling** (no "switch Pulumi to Terraform", no "move off
  GitHub Actions"). Improve how they are used.
- Compliance context: ISO 27001 (in progress), HIPAA, regional data-protection law; multiple
  insurer tenants in different countries. Sensitive data: medical records, national IDs, bank
  accounts.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents | Language |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | Entry point for graders: what the deliverable is, how to read it | English |
| `docs/` | The deliverable: framework, workflows, policies, rollout plan | English |
| `examples/` | Concrete, copy-pasteable artifacts: Claude Code settings/hooks, GitHub Actions workflows, IAM/OIDC policy sketches, plugin manifests | English |
| `diagrams/` | Architecture and workflow diagrams (source + rendered) | English labels |
| `work/` | Working notes, the challenge text (`00-challenge.md`), scratch analysis, decision log | Vietnamese or English |
| `transcripts/` | Copies of the raw Claude Code session files (`*.jsonl`) for this project, unedited | n/a |
| `CLAUDE.md` | This file | English |

Numbered prefixes (`00-`, `01-`, …) in `docs/` and `work/` define reading order. Running logs
that are not part of the reading order stay unnumbered (e.g. `work/session-log.md`).

## Rule 1 — Every claim about a tool's capability needs a source marker

The deliverable depends on what Claude Code, GitHub Actions, AWS IAM, Pulumi, k0s etc. can
actually do. Model memory is often stale. Therefore every non-trivial statement about a
feature, flag, setting, default, or limit carries one of these markers:

| Marker | Meaning | Required evidence |

# CLAUDE.md — Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1

## Purpose of this repo

This repository is my submission for Papaya's **DevSecOps Challenge 1 — "DevSecOps with
Coding Agents at Papaya"** (full text: `work/00-challenge.md`). The task is to design the
framework and workflow for how Papaya uses coding agents (Claude Code) for DevSecOps,
reconciling two positions:

- Engineering: "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly."
- Compliance: "Nothing changes in production without a named human who reviewed and approved it."

Two things make this repo unusual and shape every rule below:

1. **The complete, raw Claude Code session transcripts are part of the submission** and are
   graded. Work transparently: state the reason behind each recommendation, show trade-offs,
   and say so when something is unverified.
2. **I have no access to Papaya's systems or code**, and the challenge does not expect it.
   Everything is a design on top of the stack described in the challenge's Appendix A.

## Hard constraints from the brief

- Design for Papaya's existing stack: AWS (Lambda via Serverless Framework, ECS, EC2, Aurora
  PostgreSQL, SNS/SQS, Step Functions, S3, CloudWatch), GCP (Vertex AI, Gemini), k0s
  Kubernetes, Firebase Hosting, a single GitHub monorepo, GitHub Actions, Pulumi, Claude Code
  (Team Premium) with an internal plugin marketplace, Linear, Slack.
- **Do not propose replacing IaC or CI tooling** (no "switch Pulumi to Terraform", no "move off
  GitHub Actions"). Improve how they are used.
- Compliance context: ISO 27001 (in progress), HIPAA, regional data-protection law; multiple
  insurer tenants in different countries. Sensitive data: medical records, national IDs, bank
  accounts.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents | Language |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | Entry point for graders: what the deliverable is, how to read it | English |
| `docs/` | The deliverable: framework, workflows, policies, rollout plan | English |
| `examples/` | Concrete, copy-pasteable artifacts: Claude Code settings/hooks, GitHub Actions workflows, IAM/OIDC policy sketches, plugin manifests | English |
| `diagrams/` | Architecture and workflow diagrams (source + rendered) | English labels |
| `work/` | Working notes, the challenge text (`00-challenge.md`), scratch analysis, decision log | Vietnamese or English |
| `transcripts/` | Copies of the raw Claude Code session files (`*.jsonl`) for this project, unedited | n/a |
| `CLAUDE.md` | This file | English |

Numbered prefixes (`00-`, `01-`, …) in `docs/` and `work/` define reading order. Running logs
that are not part of the reading order stay unnumbered (e.g. `work/session-log.md`).

## Rule 1 — Every claim about a tool's capability needs a source marker

The deliverable depends on what Claude Code, GitHub Actions, AWS IAM, Pulumi, k0s etc. can
actually do. Model memory is often stale. Therefore every non-trivial statement about a
feature, flag, setting, default, or limit carries one of these markers:

| Marker | Meaning | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ | Verified in this environment | A command run in this session with its output, or a file read here |
| 📖 | Taken from official documentation | A link to the specific doc page, ideally with the version/date |
| ⚠️ | Assumption or recollection, not verified | Say what would be needed to verify it |

Rules of use:

- Never present ⚠️ content as fact. If an assumption is load-bearing for a recommendation,
  flag it in the document as an open item to verify.
- Prefer ✅ over 📖 over ⚠️. If something can be checked locally (e.g. a Claude Code setting
  on this machine), check it.
- Keep markers in the submitted docs too, not only in work notes. Graders should be able to
  see what was verified and what was not.
- When the official docs and memory disagree, docs win; note the discrepancy.
- Do not invent product features, settings keys, CLI flags, or IAM condition keys. If a
  needed capability cannot be confirmed, design around it or mark it as a dependency.

## Rule 2 — No secrets, no personal data

- No credentials, tokens, API keys, account IDs, ARNs with real account IDs, kubeconfigs,
  private keys, or `.env` contents anywhere in this repo or in the chat. Examples use obvious
  placeholders such as `<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>` or `123456789012`.
- No personal data about real people: no names of Papaya staff, no email addresses other than
  what git already records as commit author, no customer or partner data. The challenge's
  example data categories (medical documents, national IDs) are referenced only as categories.
- Transcripts are committed unedited, as the challenge requires, so **do not paste secrets
  or personal data into the chat in the first place**. Do not print environment variables,
  settings files, or shell history without redacting values. If this rule is accidentally
  broken, stop and tell the user immediately before continuing.
- The git author identity is set repo-locally (personal address) before the first push; all
  commits were rewritten to it while still unpushed. Do not change it further.
- Accepted exception (decided session 2, 2026-11-08): the committed transcripts contain the
  author's own work email addresses (from tool output and from the context Claude Code
  injects). They are kept unedited because the challenge requires raw transcripts; no other
  person's data is involved.

## Rule 3 — Language

- **Submitted material** (`README.md`, everything in `docs/`, `examples/`, `diagrams/`,
  commit messages, code comments) is in **English**.
- **Working notes** in `work/` may be in Vietnamese or English, but every working note starts
  with an `## English summary` section (about 5–10 lines) directly under its title, so graders
  can follow the reasoning without reading Vietnamese. The summary only restates what the note
  already says. (Agreed 2026-11-09.)

## Decisions taken so far

content.content:
The page doesn't list "Vertex AI," "Gemini API on Vertex AI," or "Vertex AI Search" by name. It does list related entries:

- "Generative AI on Agent Platform"
- "Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform"
- "Agent Search on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform"
- "Vertex AI Workbench instances"

The page doesn't say whether these map to the products you named, so confirm with Google before relying on them for PHI.

**1. Is Admin Activity always on?** Yes. The page says: "Admin Activity audit logs are always written; you can't configure, exclude, or disable them."

**2. Are Data Access logs disabled by default, except for BigQuery?** Yes. The page says: "Except for BigQuery, Data Access audit logs are disabled by default because they can generate large volumes of data."

**3. How do you enable them?** The page doesn't give console steps. It says that for services other than BigQuery, "you must explicitly enable them," and links to the "Enable Data Access audit logs" instructions. For Google Cloud MCP servers, you turn on audit logging for `mcp.googleapis.com` in the IAM `AuditConfig` object. Enabling them may add charges, since the page warns that enabling "might result in your Google Cloud project being charged for additional log usage."

**Training:** Google won't use your data for training by default. The page states: "Google won't use your data to train or fine-tune any AI/ML models without your prior permission or instruction." This applies to all managed models, including GA and pre-GA models.

Caching doesn't change this. For implicit caching, the page says data "is never used to train or fine-tune models." The same wording appears for OpenAI flagship models: "Customer data is never used to train or fine-tune models."

**HIPAA:** The page doesn't mention HIPAA, so it doesn't say whether HIPAA applies to these services. Check with your Google Cloud account team or the related compliance documentation.

**Time-bound bindings with `request.time`**

- The article gives this example for a role binding that grants access until a fixed moment: "request.time < timestamp('2021-01-01T00:00:00Z')"
- Timestamps use RFC 3339 format, and time zones use IANA Time Zone Database identifiers.
- For temporary access, the article points to a separate guide, "Configuring temporary access."

**Limits**

- **Conditions per policy:** The article gives a best practice, not a hard cap: "don't add more than 100 conditional role bindings to a single allow policy." Exceeding this can push you past the allow policy size limit.
- **Expression size:** The article doesn't state a maximum expression size.
- **Supported resources:** "Only some resource types accept conditions in role bindings." For other resource types, you can grant conditional access by granting roles at the organization or project level.
- **Cloud Storage:** "To use conditions in the allow policy for a Cloud Storage bucket, you must" enable uniform bucket-level access on the bucket. If you can't, add the conditional grant to a higher-level resource, such as the project.
- **Restricted roles:** Conditions can't be used with legacy basic roles or with `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`.

**What PAM does:** Privileged Access Manager provides temporary, just-in-time privilege elevation for selected principals. An administrator creates an entitlement that sets who can request access, which roles are granted, and the maximum grant length. Requesters receive the roles for a limited window, after which PAM removes them.
- Quote: "control just-in-time temporary privilege elevation for select principals" (the page's description of PAM's purpose)

**Approval workflow:** Approvals are optional and set per entitlement. Administrators can require sequential approval levels, with up to two levels and five approvers per level, which is a Preview feature.
- Quote: "Whether requests need approval from a select set of principals" (the optional approval setting)
- Quote: "allowing up to two levels of sequential approvals for each entitlement" (Preview multi-level approvals)

**Maximum grant duration:** Each entitlement sets its own limit. The page doesn't give a fixed maximum value.
- Quote: "The maximum duration a grant can last." (entitlement attribute)

**Audit logging:** PAM events are recorded in Cloud Audit Logs, which lets you review who had access, when, and why.
- Quote: "are logged to Cloud Audit Logs" (PAM events such as entitlement creation and grant reviews)
- Grant records are deleted 30 days after a grant ends, but the logs are kept for the `_Required` bucket's retention period.

**GA/preview status:** The page doesn't label base PAM as GA. It marks several features as Preview, including multi-level approvals, scope customization, service account approvals, inheritance, notification customization, grant scheduling, and grant withdrawal.
- Quote: "Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support." (the Preview disclaimer)

**Pricing:** The page doesn't mention pricing. Some features require the Enterprise or Premium tier of Security Command Center.

**Permissions**
- Only some permissions can be denied, and the list is in the "Permissions supported in deny policies" page.
- Permission groups can deny sets of permissions using wildcards, but only in supported groups: "You can only use wildcards in supported permission groups."
- A group covers future permissions too: "Permission groups include all current and future permissions that match the specified pattern."

**Principals**
- Denied principals can be individuals (user accounts, service accounts, single workforce or workload identities) or sets, such as "Google groups, Cloud Identity domains" and "all users on the internet."

**Exceptions**
- `exceptionPrincipals` exempts principals from the rule, even if they are denied directly or through a group: "These principals are not denied the specified permissions even if they are listed in".
- `exceptionPermissions` lets principals use specific permissions that fall within `deniedPermissions`, such as exceptions within a permission group.

**Conditions**
- `denialConditions` are optional. The rule applies when the condition is true or can't be evaluated.
- Conditions only recognize resource tag functions: "denial conditions only recognize resource tag functions."

**Limits**
- Deny policies attach only to organizations, folders, or projects, and are inherited by lower-level resources.
- Each resource can have up to 500 deny policies.
- Those policies can contain 500 deny rules in total.
- Changes take time to propagate, since access changes are "eventually consistent."
- A deny policy on a higher level still applies even if lower-level policies are more permissive.

content.content:
**Yes, `firebaseServiceAccount` is required.** The page lists it as "`firebaseServiceAccount` _{string}_ (required)" and describes it as "This is a service account JSON key."

**No.** The page doesn't mention Workload Identity Federation or GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS. It only says the key can be set up with `firebase init hosting:github` or created manually, and it should be stored as an encrypted secret named `FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT`.

**Enabled by default:** Admin Activity and System Event logs. The document says, "You can't disable Admin Activity audit logs," and "System Event audit logs are always enabled; you can't disable them."

**Data Access logs:** Not enabled by default. The document says, "Data Access audit logs are disabled by default and aren't written unless explicitly enabled."

**generateContent:** Yes, it is logged. The audited operations table lists "endpoints.generateContent" under Data Access (DATA_READ) audit logs. Because Data Access logs must be explicitly enabled, you would need to turn them on to capture this.

The document refers to "Agent Platform" rather than "Vertex AI," so I've applied its terms to your question.

**Using the Google Cloud console**

1. Go to the **Audit Logs** page in IAM & Admin, then select a project, folder, or organization.
2. In the **Data Access audit logs configuration** table, select the services you want. The docs note that "select the Data Access audit log types that you want to enable for your selected services" (in the Permission types tab).
3. Click **Save**. A check icon in the table confirms the audit logs are enabled.

To enable logging for every service that produces Data Access logs, select all services in the table instead.

**Using IAM policy `auditConfigs` (gcloud)**

1. Read the current policy: `gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID > /tmp/policy.yaml`
2. Add or change only the `auditConfigs` section. As the docs put it, "Change (or add) only the `auditConfigs` section."
3. Write the policy back: `gcloud projects set-iam-policy PROJECT_ID /tmp/policy.yaml`

For example, this YAML enables `DATA_WRITE` logs for Cloud SQL:

```yaml
auditConfigs:
- auditLogConfigs:
  - logType: DATA_WRITE
  service: cloudsql.googleapis.com
```

Use `service: allServices` to apply a configuration to all services. Valid log types are `ADMIN_READ`, `DATA_READ`, and `DATA_WRITE`.

**Using the API**

Call `getIamPolicy`, edit `auditConfigs` while preserving `etag`, then call `setIamPolicy` with `updateMask` set to `auditConfigs,etag`.

**Cautions**

- "Your edited IAM policy replaces the current policy." Keep the `bindings` and `etag` sections intact, or you could lose access to the project.
- With the API, "You must specify the `updateMask` parameter as shown."
- Data Access logs can add significant logging charges.

**Max grant duration**
- Entitlements cap grants at seven days: "The maximum duration you can set for an entitlement is 7 days."
- The gcloud and REST docs set the range from 30 minutes to 7 days: "The supported range is between 30 minutes (`1800s`) and 168 hours (`604800s`)."

**Approval settings**
- You can skip approvals entirely by choosing "Activate access without approvals."
- Multi-level approval requires Security Command Center Premium or Enterprise tier, and it "allowing up to two levels of sequential approvals for each entitlement."
- Each approval level can require up to five approvals: "You can mandate up to five approvals per level."
- Each approval can list up to 20 approving principals: "You can add up to 20 approving principals (identities or groups) per approval."
- A denial ends the request: "If any approver denies the grant, then the grant moves to the `denied` state."

**Justification**
- Requesters can be required to justify their request, which is a setting you choose when creating the entitlement.
- Approvers can also be required to justify their decisions: "To require approvers to enter justifications for approving requests."
- In the API, approver justification is set with "requireApproverJustification": true.

**Workload Identity Federation (WIF) usage**

- The page says "Workload Identity Federation is recommended over Service Account Keys" because it avoids exporting a long-lived credential.
- Three setups are offered: direct WIF (preferred), WIF through a service account, and Service Account Key JSON.
- `workload_identity_provider` is required and must be the full provider identifier, including project number, pool, and provider.
- Providing `service_account` switches from direct WIF to WIF through a service account.
- `audience` defaults to the `workload_identity_provider` value.
- Derived credentials are short-lived, since "the GitHub OIDC token expires in 5 minutes."
- To generate OAuth 2.0 or ID tokens, you must supply a service account email, and the pool needs `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser` on that account.
- The example workflow sets `id-token: 'write'` under `permissions`.

**Firebase**

- The page warns that WIF is "not supported by Firebase Admin SDK." It advises using Service Account Key JSON authentication instead.

**Application Default Credentials (ADC)**

- The page does not mention ADC by name. It does describe the `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` variable, covered below.

**Credentials file and GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS**

- With `create_credentials_file` enabled (the default), the action can "securely generate a credentials file which can be used for authentication via gcloud and Google Cloud SDKs."
- The file is written to `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE`, and "The file is automatically removed at the end of the job via a post action."
- When `create_credentials_file` is true, the action also exports `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, along with `CLOUDSDK_AUTH_CREDENTIAL_FILE_OVERRIDE` and `GOOGLE_GHA_CREDS_PATH`.
- `actions/checkout` must run first, because it is needed for the credentials file to be exported correctly.
- `cleanup_credentials` defaults to true and removes created credentials when the job completes.
- Prerequisites say to add `gha-creds-*.json` to ignore files so credentials are not committed.

content.content: AWS Chatbot is now Amazon Q Developer. [Learn more](service-rename.md) # What is Amazon Q Developer in chat applications? Amazon Q Developer in chat applications enables DevOps and software development teams to use messaging program chat channels to monitor and respond to operational events in their AWS Cloud. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications processes AWS service notifications from Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS), and forwards them to chat channels so teams can analyze and act on them immediately, regardless of location. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications also supports AWS CLI commands so you can manage AWS resources directly from your chat channels. **Topics** + [Features of Amazon Q Developer in chat applications](#chatbot-benefits) + [How Amazon Q Developer in chat applications works](#chatbot-works) + [Amazon Q Developer in chat applications rename - Summary of changes](service-rename.md) + [Regions and quotas for Amazon Q Developer in chat applications](chatbot-regions.md) + [Supported services for Amazon Q Developer in chat applications](chatbot-services.md) + [Amazon Q Developer in chat applications requirements](#chatbot-requirements) + [Accessing Amazon Q Developer in chat applications](#chatbot-access) ## Features of Amazon Q Developer in chat applications Amazon Q Developer in chat applications enables ChatOps for AWS. *ChatOps* speeds software development and operations by enabling DevOps teams to use chat clients and chatbots to communicate and execute tasks. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications notifies chat users about events in their AWS services, so teams can collaboratively monitor and resolve issues in real time, instead of addressing emails from their SNS topics. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications also allows you to format incident metrics from Amazon CloudWatch as charts for viewing in chat notifications. Important features of the Amazon Q Developer in chat applications service include the following: + **Ask Amazon Q** – You can get Amazon Q Developer, Generative Artifical Intelligence (AI) assistant powered answers to your AWS questions directly in your chat channels. For more information about see [Chatting with Amazon Q Developer in chat channels](asking-questions.md). + **Supports Amazon Chime, Microsoft Teams, and Slack** – You can add Amazon Q Developer in chat applications to your Amazon Chime chat rooms, Microsoft Teams channels, or Slack channels in just a few clicks. + **Predefined AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy templates** – Amazon Q Developer in chat applications provides chat room-specific permission controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). The available predefined templates make it easy to select and set up the permissions you want associated with a given channel or chat room. + **Receive notifications** – Use Amazon Q Developer in chat applications to receive notifications about operational incidents and other events from supported sources, such as operational alarms, security alerts, or budget deviations. To set up notifications in the Amazon Q Developer in chat applications console, choose the channels or chat rooms you want to receive notifications and then choose which Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics should trigger notifications. + **Customize notifications** – You can define and receive customized AWS service and application notifications directly in your chat channels. Custom notifications can be as succint or comprehensive you desire and use the same Amazon SNS-based mechanisms as default notifications. + **Create custom actions** – Custom actions transform your notifications into actionable items. A custom action appears as a button on your notifications. This button represents a Lambda function or CLI command that you define. You can use custom actions to retrieve telemetry information, run Lambda functions, run an automation runbook, and notify team members. When an issue arises, you can easily take action directly from your notifications. + **Monitor and manage AWS resources through the AWS CLI with Microsoft Teams and Slack** – Amazon Q Developer in chat applications supports CLI commands for most AWS services, making it easy to monitor and manage your AWS resources from your chat clients on desktop and mobile devices. Your teams can retrieve diagnostic information in real-time, change your AWS resources, run AWS SSM runbooks, and start long running jobs from a centralized location. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications commands use the standard AWS Command Line Interface syntax. + **Supports developer tools** – You can manage your Amazon Q Developer in chat applications resources using developer tools such as AWS software development kits (SDKs), the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK), AWS CloudFormation, and AWS Cloud Control API. You can also use third party infrastructure as code (IaaC) providers such as [Terraform](https://www.hashicorp.com/blog/managing-resources-with-the-terraform-aws-cloud-control-provider). ## How Amazon Q Developer in chat applications works Amazon Q Developer in chat applications uses Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics to send event and alarm notifications from AWS services to your chat channels. Once an SNS topic is associated with a configured chat client, events and alarms from various services are processed and notifications are delivered to the specified chat channels and webhooks. For Microsoft Teams and Slack, after an administrator approves Amazon Q Developer in chat applications support for the tenant or workspace, anyone in the team or workspace can add Amazon Q Developer in chat applications to their chat channels. For Amazon Chime, users with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to use Amazon Chime can add Amazon Q Developer in chat applications to their webhooks. You use the Amazon Q Developer in chat applications console to configure chat clients to receive notifications from SNS topics. You can also run AWS CLI commands directly in chat channels using Amazon Q Developer. You can retrieve diagnostic information, configure AWS resources, and run workflows. To run a command, Amazon Q Developer in chat applications checks that all required parameters are entered. If any are missing, Amazon Q Developer in chat applications prompts you for the required information. Amazon Q Developer in chat applications then confirms if the command is permissible by checking the command against what is allowed by the configured IAM roles and the channel guardrail policies. For more information, see [Running AWS CLI commands from chat channels](chatbot-cli-commands.md) and [Understanding permissions](understanding-permissions.md). ## Amazon Q Developer in chat applications requirements To use Amazon Q Developer in chat applications, you need the following: + An AWS account to associate with Amazon Chime, Microsoft Teams, or Slack chat clients during Amazon Q Developer in chat applications setup. + Administrative privileges for your Amazon Chime chat room, Microsoft Teams tenant, or Slack workspace. You can be the Slack workspace owner or have the ability to work with workspace owners to get approval for installing Amazon Q Developer in chat applications. + Familiarity with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and IAM roles and policies. For more information about IAM, see [What is IAM?](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/) in the *IAM User Guide*. + Experience with the AWS services supported by Amazon Q Developer in chat applications, including experience configuring those services to subscribe to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topics to send notifications. For information about supported services, see [Using Amazon Q Developer in chat applications with Other AWS Services](related-services.md). To access Amazon CloudWatch metrics, Amazon Q Developer in chat applications requires an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role with a permissions policy and a trust policy. You create this IAM role, with the required policies, [using the Amazon Q Developer in chat applications console](https://us-east-2.console.aws.amazon.com/chatbot/home?region=us-east-2#/chat-clients). You can use an existing IAM role, but it must have the required policies. ## Accessing Amazon Q Developer in chat applications You access and configure Amazon Q Developer in chat applications through the Amazon Q Developer in chat applications console at [https://console.aws.amazon.com/chatbot/](https://console.aws.amazon.com/chatbot/). When you subscribe an endpoint to a topic, you can publish a notification to the topic and Amazon SNS sends an HTTP POST request delivering the contents of the notification to the subscribed endpoint. When you subscribe the endpoint, you choose whether Amazon SNS uses HTTP or HTTPS to send the POST request to the endpoint. If you use HTTPS, then you can take advantage of the support in Amazon SNS for the following: + **Server Name Indication (SNI)**—This allows Amazon SNS to support HTTPS endpoints that require SNI, such as a server requiring multiple certificates for hosting multiple domains. For more information about SNI, see [Server Name Indication](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Server_Name_Indication). + **Basic and Digest Access Authentication**—This allows you to specify a username and password in the HTTPS URL for the HTTP POST request, such as `https://user:password@domain.com` or `https://user@domain.com` The username and password are encrypted over the SSL connection established when using HTTPS. Only the domain name is sent in plaintext. For more information about Basic and Digest Access Authentication, see [RFC-2617](http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2617). **Important** Amazon SNS does not currently support private HTTP(S) endpoints. HTTPS URLs are only retrievable from the Amazon SNS `GetSubscriptionAttributes` API action, for principals to which you have granted API access. **Note** The client service must be able to support the `HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized` header response The request contains the subject and message that were published to the topic along with metadata about the notification in a JSON document.
